goal: Enum constructors are written qualified (SchoolPerson.Teacher) instead of bare (Teacher) after importing the enum

extra_axes.name: language
extra_axes.why: the goal is a syntax rule; its cost is in how code reads, what users and models expect, and which errors exist
extra_axes.ruling_why: every claim that could change the decision is about readability, TypeScript habits or ambiguity, none of which fits device, time or tokens

claims.text: selfhost (18 files, 7.5k lines): 0 qualified constructor uses, about 190 bare user-enum constructors in expressions, about 160 bare Some/None/Ok/Err, about 500 in patterns. testdata (333 files): 21 qualified. Regex heuristic, counts are approximate.

The compiler already reports an ambiguous bare constructor at the use site ('constructor Low is ambiguous: A, B all have it; write A.Low') and resolves a bare name from the expected type (const y: B = Low compiles).

A local named like a constructor hides it silently: in shadow.nra `const Low = 5` makes `Low` the int. It errors only because the types differ; with a matching type it would compile with a different meaning.
D2: syntax follows TypeScript, and 'the same text never means two different things'. TypeScript enum members are always written Color.Red.

Prior art: Rust requires Enum::Variant unless `use Enum::*`, and re-exports Some/None/Ok/Err bare in its prelude. Swift allows `.teacher` when the type is known. OCaml, Haskell and Gleam use bare constructors; Gleam imports them by name. TypeScript and Kotlin qualify.

evidence.source: Rust reference (paths, prelude), Swift book (implicit member expressions), Gleam tour (imports), TS handbook (enums)

claims.text: 21 selfhost nodes are todo, including the six selfhost-check-bodies nodes just split. A migration that rewrites selfhost/*.nra touches files those nodes will edit.

Outside patterns, a user enum's constructors are written qualified: SchoolPerson.Teacher, SchoolPerson.Student("x"). Importing SchoolPerson is enough. Some, None, Ok and Err stay bare as prelude names.

evidence.source: J4, J5: TypeScript and Rust both qualify; Rust keeps the prelude four bare

claims.text: In match arms and `is` patterns the bare name stays legal, because it is resolved from the subject's type and cannot be ambiguous; the qualified form is also accepted there.

evidence.source: J2: subject-type resolution already exists; J1: about 500 pattern sites keep working

claims.user_why: one rule: constructors are always qualified, patterns included (Q1)

claims.text: A bare constructor in an expression, and `import { Teacher }`, give an error with an exact fix (write SchoolPerson.Teacher / import SchoolPerson), as other TypeScript-habit errors do.

evidence.source: compiler/internal/narra/CLAUDE.md: TypeScript-habit errors carry errorfFix and a testdata/diagnostics case

claims.text: This removes the ambiguity rule the spec never finished (what counts as ambiguous, shadowing by locals), since an expression constructor always names its enum.
Keep bare constructors, and only add the import fix and spell out the ambiguity and shadowing rules.
claims.ruling_why: J3 shows a local can silently change what a bare constructor means, which D2 forbids; the alternative keeps that hazard and still needs the unwritten ambiguity rule

claims.text: About 190 selfhost sites and about 400 testdata sites must be rewritten, and the selfhost rewrite collides with the todo selfhost nodes.
P3's fix is exact, so the migration is the compiler applying its own fixes: one mechanical pull request, landed between selfhost waves.

evidence.source: testdata/diagnostics harness applies fixes and recompiles (compiler CLAUDE.md)

claims.text: Qualified names stutter where enums already prefix their constructors: Type.TStruct, Token.TokIdent. Code gets longer, and the prefixes become redundant, which invites a rename across selfhost.

evidence.source: J1 top bare names: TVoid, TokIdent, TokPunct, TInt

claims.text: The prefixes exist to dodge bare-name clashes (J2's ambiguity error). Qualified access lets them go: Type.Struct, Token.Ident. The rename is optional and can follow later.

evidence.source: J1 clash list: Struct/Enum/Trait in two enums each

claims.text: Two rules to learn: qualified in expressions, bare allowed in patterns. Users may wonder why `Teacher =>` works but `const t = Teacher` does not.
claims.ruling_why: this is a taste call between consistency and match brevity; Rust is the reverse (qualified in both) and Swift allows .x in both; the user decides (Q1)
claims.user_why: two rules are worse than longer match arms (Q1)

claims.text: Swift-style `.Teacher` wherever the expected type is known (arguments, annotated consts, returns, patterns), and SchoolPerson.Teacher elsewhere.
claims.ruling_why: it shortens the common case but is new syntax with no TypeScript precedent (J4); it can be added later without breaking P1, so it needs the user's call, not a ruling now

claims.text: The prelude exception (Some/None/Ok/Err bare, user enums qualified) is a special case a reader must know.

evidence.source: J5: Rust has the same exception and it is not a common complaint

claims.text: With Q1, the migration also covers the about 500 pattern sites, so about 1,100 sites in total. All are rewritten by applying the P3 fix.

questions.ask: Inside match arms and `is` patterns, may enum constructors stay bare (`Teacher =>`), or must they be qualified there too (`SchoolPerson.Teacher =>`)?
Add Swift-style `.Teacher` shorthand where the expected type is known, now, later, or never?
With SchoolPerson.Teacher, an import alias equal to an enum name makes SchoolPerson.X mean two things. D67 lets an alias equal a type name (import * as Array from "std/array"). Keep that?
questions.answer: No. TypeScript rejects an import that conflicts with a local declaration. An import alias may not equal any type name visible in the module. Same-named constructors across enums (Maybe.None vs prelude None) and duplicate constructors within one enum: fine as proposed.

questions.ask: Conventional alias for std modules whose type is capitalized (Array, Map, Box, Range, Option, Result)?
questions.answer: Plural aliases, paths unchanged: Arrays, Maps, Boxes, Ranges, Options, Results.

questions.ask: Should named imports accept renaming (import { map as mapArray } from "std/array"), so the plural namespace alias is only a convention?
questions.answer: Yes. Add { a as b } to named imports (amends D25).
